title: Fly.io runs everything today. Supabase holds identity only.
recommendation: One Fly.io Machine in region iad serves the website, the account pages, the /api/v1 interface and the Model Context Protocol endpoint from one origin, and keeps every durable record on one encrypted volume. Supabase is the identity provider and holds two accounts; it holds no application table and no storage bucket. Resend holds the sender domains. Stripe holds payments and the live account is active. Customers run their harnesses and supply their model endpoints, so no model-hosting hardware is required. Moving the records and the files to Supabase is still the plan for a paid public launch, and that work is not done.
status: Fly release 10 serves the website and the service at https://app.baltor.ai, https://baltor.ai, https://www.baltor.ai and https://baltor-pilot.fly.dev. One Machine in iad runs image digest sha256:a2d31be0, which releases 8, 9 and 10 all share; releases 9 and 10 restarted that same image after deployment secrets were staged. The service still keeps every durable record in SQLite and in files on one encrypted 1 GB volume, so one Machine is the only writer. Browser sign-in, operator-provisioned client access and the billing webhook, checkout and customer portal are switched on, and public registration is still closed. Live payments are activated on a separate live Stripe account, so a charge is now possible; the earlier note on this page that live charging was disabled is no longer true. Customer signup, shared storage, billing and complete native task execution are not qualified, because no real card has completed a subscription and no customer journey has been run from end to end. This is not a qualified paid release. Automatic deployment from GitHub stays off; the pilot workflow runs only when a person starts it.

operations.title: How to deploy
steps: Commit to main and wait for the continuous integration run on that exact revision to pass. The workflow reads the run and refuses a revision that has no successful run of its own.

Set the pilot environment values: the organization, the application, the primary region, the approved monthly allowance and the approval reference, and set the deployment switch to true. A missing or malformed value stops the run before anything is built.
Start the workflow named Baltor Fly pilot by hand, choose deploy, and retype baltor-pilot into the confirmation field. It runs only from main, and only one run at a time.

The run installs the pinned Fly command line and checks its digest, confirms the application exists in the approved organization, requires exactly one Machine and the one volume in the primary region, and validates fly.toml strictly.
It builds the image from Dockerfile.service and runs the container checks with no provider access, then reads main again and refuses if the branch moved while the image was building.

It pushes the image, reads the exact digest back, and deploys by that digest with one Machine, the immediate strategy, no retries and no new public addresses. It then reads /api/v1/health and requires healthy true.

Write a release record beside pilot-release-8.json with the revision, the digest, the release kept for rollback and the checks that ran, then set the deployment switch back to false. A deployment without a record cannot be rolled back from the repository alone.

operations.title: How to roll back
steps: Decide first whether the image, the host configuration or the data is wrong, and write down why. Restarting the Machine undoes none of them.

Wrong image: deploy the previous digest with the same configuration. The Fly release list names every digest, and sha256:7b45d327 from release 7 is the most recent image that differs from the one running. An old image on its own is not a complete rollback.

Wrong host configuration: restore the backup of /data/host.json on the volume and restart the Machine. The release number does not change when only that file changes, so the release list will not show the fault and will not show the repair.

Wrong data: restore a volume snapshot. Five daily snapshots are kept. A snapshot restores the tenants, the key digests, the grants, the usage and the billing state together; they cannot be restored separately, so a restore can withdraw access that was granted after the snapshot.
Reconcile the staged secrets by name afterwards. A secret that a rolled-back image does not expect is still staged, and staging or removing one restarts the Machine and creates another release.
Record the rollback beside the release record it undoes, and keep the failed attempt next to it.

operations.title: How to read the logs
steps: An authorized session reads the application log through the Fly connection; ask it for the application baltor-pilot. The same log is on the Fly dashboard for the baltor organization, and from the Fly command line with the credential named fly.

Four kinds of line matter. runner lines show the image being pulled, the encrypted volume being opened and the Machine starting. app lines are the service itself. health lines show the check failing at every restart and passing a second or two later, which is normal. proxy lines are requests that never reached the service.
Compare a restart in the log with the release list. A restart with the line Container image already prepared and no new digest means a secret or the host configuration changed, not the code.
The log carries no key, no authorization header and no tenant body. Keep it that way: do not paste a line into a report without reading it first.
Fly keeps only a short window of lines. Save the lines that matter into a report under a new name rather than expecting to read them again later.

alternatives.tradeoff: This is what runs. It fits your experience and keeps ordinary compute separate from managed data and identity. Engineering owns deployment, health checks, restore tests and sizing. Only compute and identity are actually on it today.

A 1 CPU / 2 GB web service is $25 each month. Workspace fees are separate: Hobby is $0 plus compute, Pro is $25 plus compute. It was originally preferred for its predictable fixed-size service, not because it was measured against Fly.io.
Pro has a $20 monthly minimum including $20 of usage, then additional resource usage. Convenient container deployment; memory and sustained processor use make the bill variable.

Useful for a separate frontend, but not required by this packaged Python site, which serves its own website from the same origin. Its free Hobby plan is for personal, non-commercial use; do not assume it covers a paid product.

alternatives.fit: Add only after a measured retrieval need
alternatives.tradeoff: Keep the backend replaceable. The running service uses SQLite full-text search today. Add a dedicated index when relevance, feature requirements, corpus size or latency justify another service, not because every retrieval project has one.

engineering: Write a release record for every deployment. Releases 9 and 10 changed the running service and left no record, so the repository cannot say what changed or what to roll back to.

Wire the verified sender: stage the email credential as a deployment secret, add sending at the existing boundary, then test confirmation and recovery against a controlled recipient. The service sends no email today.

Implement and test PostgreSQL against the existing catalogue contract, including atomic read-set writes, idempotency, revocation and uncertain-commit recovery. Do not create two competing authoritative tenant stores.

Build the retrieval projection with metadata filters, full-text search, typo handling and a versioned embedding space. PostgreSQL full-text ranking, pgvector and optional reranking must remain separate configurable stages.
Create the private bucket and connect it to exact artifact references. Authorize each selected body before issuing a short-lived delivery grant; a signed link can remain usable until its expiry.

Qualify backup restoration, rollback, failed payment and client reconnection. Model Context Protocol transport is stateless, but durable application state still needs the shared database before a second serving instance.

connection_note: Supabase documents direct connections for persistent backends with IPv6, including Fly.io. This matters only after the records move; the running service opens no database connection to Supabase today. Use a bounded application-side pool and verified TLS. If the actual route is IPv4-only, use the dashboard's session-pooler connection string. Do not guess a pooler hostname, and do not use transaction pooling for session features such as LISTEN/NOTIFY.
